backTranslations.41:
**Before the appointment**
- Enter the date of the appointment in the 'Appointment' tab. MenoMap shows you how far along your notes are and what would make them more meaningful.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most to you. Limit yourself to three or four.
- Create your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check whether your medication list is up to date.

**At the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed so that it can be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks a different language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

They are a summary of what you entered, plus anything you imported from Apple Health. They are not a diagnosis and not a complete medical record, and patterns in them are only a look at things happening at the same time, not proof of a cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Enter new medications with their start date. In a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries before and after, which makes the next check-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day on which 12 months in a row passed with no period, without something else explaining it (such as a pregnancy, some medications or a surgery). In many countries it falls on average in the early 50s, but anything between the mid 40s and mid 50s is common.

**Perimenopause** covers the years up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so the period can become irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many changes that people associate with the change years, such as hot flashes, night sweats, altered sleep and mood swings, often begin already here, while the period still comes. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer, and it goes differently for every person.

**Postmenopause** is everything after this 12-month mark. Some symptoms settle over time, others can persist for years.

Menopause can also occur earlier, for example through an operation in which the ovaries are removed, through some cancer treatments or through other conditions. A menopause before 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth talking to a doctor about it.

**How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, doctors recognise perimenopause or menopause from your history and your symptoms. Blood tests are not always necessary because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. They are more likely to be used when someone is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap can and cannot do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which phase you are in. What it can do: honestly record what you notice, meaning waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with skin flushing, sweating, racing heart or subsequent chills. Night sweats are the same during sleep, and it can be so strong that you wake up from it or your bedding is soaked through.

They are among the most common changes around the change years. Some have a few mild ones, others many per day that disrupt work and sleep. In some they fade within a few years, in others they last considerably longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, warm rooms, stress or heavy bedding. This differs very much from person to person, so it can be more useful to follow your own markers than a general list.

**There are other causes too.** Skin flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern or come with weight loss, fever or feeling ill, bring it up with a doctor.

**Describing them well.** Useful details for an appointment:
- How many per day and at night, roughly
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, sport
- What seems to precede them
- What you have tried and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's wave button and adding entries afterwards are made exactly for recording this without much effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options as well as practical approaches. Which of them suit you is a topic for a conversation with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone replacement therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces part of the estrogen that the body produces less of around the change years. Major guidelines describe it for many people as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. Those who still have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen in addition to the estrogen, to protect the uterine lining.

**Benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, how long ago the last period was, personal history and family history (for example with breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) as well as the type and route of administration of the treatment. That is why it is a decision you make with a doctor who knows your history, and not something an app can decide.

**Questions that are often asked:**
- Is hormone replacement therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- Which type and form would you suggest, and why?
- What benefit could I expect, and how quickly?
- What risks do I personally have, and how do they compare with no treatment?
- What should I watch for, and when should we review it?

**If you already use it,** enter it in MenoMap (Me → Medications). MenoMap shows your waves before and after the start, as a look at things happening at the same time and not as proof, so that you have something concrete to discuss at the check-up.

MenoMap never suggests starting a medication, stopping it or changing anything about it.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone replacement therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people simply prefer other ways. There are several.

**Prescription options.** For some non-hormonal medications there is evidence that they reduce hot flashes. These include certain medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer class of active ingredient developed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talk therapy and mind-body approaches.** For cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted to the change years there is evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less distressing and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that many find helpful:**
- Clothing in layers that you can take off quickly
- A fan at the desk and at the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Recognising and reducing personal triggers (the markers and experiments in MenoMap help with this)
- Regular exercise and a steady sleep rhythm

**Dietary supplements and herbal remedies.** For many of them the evidence is mixed or thin, the quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or your pharmacy what you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change after the other.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own entries before and during a change, and that is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is hard to recall on the spot a whole month full of nights. One tends to remember the most recent or the worst days. A simple record closes this gap.

**What a diary shows your doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not just that they occur
- Whether it is getting better, worse or staying the same
- What was going on around it: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point for comparison when you try a treatment

**Keep it simple.** A diary only helps if you also keep it. MenoMap is built around a one-tap wave button and an evening check-in with four questions. That costs seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks are a good start.** Two to four weeks of entries usually show a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you would like to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. The 'Appointment' tab in MenoMap helps you choose questions and prints them together with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
If you have had no period for 12 months, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked out by a doctor**, even if it occurred only once and even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brownish discharge.

Mostly the cause turns out not to be serious. A thinning vaginal or uterine lining, for example, is common. But a bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when it is found early. That is why public health recommendations advise having it examined rather than waiting.

**If you use hormone replacement therapy,** certain bleeding patterns can be expected depending on the preparation. A bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, is heavier than usual or occurs at the wrong time should also be checked out.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or your doctor's practice and say that you had a bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can record that for you (Me → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding occurred. It reminds you to have it checked out, and includes it in your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is among the most common complaints in midlife, and it rarely has only one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly or cause you to be too hot or too damp to settle again.

**Other common factors:**
- Having to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help with falling asleep but often makes the second half of the night restless
- Caffeine later in the day
- Pain, restless legs or the partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea (worth raising, especially if you are very tired during the day)

**What helps many.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and clothing in layers that you can take off; a fixed wake-up time; and less alcohol shortly before bedtime. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What you can record.** For a week or two note your sleep score, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and wave log do this with a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from Apple Health next to your night sweats, as context and not as an explanation.

**When you should have it checked out.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example when driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice that you have pauses in breathing at night or gasp for air.
